paragraphs.heading: A small crustacean in huge swarms
paragraphs.text: Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) is a species of krill living in the Antarctic waters of the Southern Ocean. It is a small crustacean that swims in large schools called swarms, which sometimes pack 10,000 to 30,000 animals into a single cubic metre. It grows to 6 centimetres long, weighs up to 2 grams and can live for up to six years. With a combined mass of roughly 500 million metric tons, it ranks among the most abundant animal species on the planet, though it is suffering from overfishing.

paragraphs.heading: A filter basket made of legs
paragraphs.text: Krill eat mostly phytoplankton, especially tiny diatoms about 20 μm across. Six legs on the krill's thorax form a "feeding basket" that strains these cells out of open water, with gaps as small as 1 μm in its finest parts. When food is scarce, the krill pushes the open basket through the water for more than half a metre, then combs the algae toward its mouth with bristles. No other animal of its size can eat such tiny phytoplankton cells directly. Krill also catch copepods, amphipods and other small zooplankton.

paragraphs.heading: Grazing under the ice
paragraphs.text: Krill can also scrape off the green layer of algae that grows on the underside of pack ice. Rake-like bristles at the tips of their legs let them graze the ice in a zig-zag, and one krill can clear a square foot in about 10 minutes. This ice algae covers vast areas and often holds far more carbon than the whole water column beneath it. It gives krill a rich supply of energy, especially in spring after food has been scarce all winter.

paragraphs.heading: Shrinking to survive
paragraphs.text: Like all crustaceans, krill must moult to grow, shedding their outer skeleton about every 13 to 20 days. Unfed krill do something exceptional for animals this size: they shrink after moulting. This is likely an adaptation to winter, when food under the ice is limited in the dark months. Their compound eyes do not shrink, so a krill whose eyes look too big for its body is a sign of starvation.

paragraphs.heading: From sinking eggs to the surface
paragraphs.text: The main spawning season runs from January to March. A female lays 6,000 to 10,000 eggs at a time, and they are fertilised as they leave her body. In the classic account, the eggs develop while sinking, and the young larva later starts a climb toward the surface called the developmental ascent. The climb is finished after three weeks, and krill reach maturity after two to three years.

paragraphs.heading: Messy eaters that move carbon
paragraphs.text: Krill are untidy feeders. They often spit out clumps of phytoplankton, called spitballs, made of thousands of cells stuck together. Their gut is a straight tube that does not digest food very efficiently, so their fecal strings still carry plenty of carbon along with diatom shells. Both the spitballs and the strings are heavy and sink very fast into the abyss.
